events.objective: Establish the precise symptom timeline and blast radius for the order-service failure: when exactly did order submit error rate and 504s begin (minute-level onset, and did it start before or after the v2.15.2 rollout?), which order-service endpoints/error signatures dominate (504 vs 4xx vs timeouts vs connection refused), and which other services show simultaneous error/latency/resource degradation (upstream callers, downstream payment/inventory/shipping/checkout, databases, gateways). Also report resource trends (CPU, memory, connection pools, saturation) for order-service and any service it calls, to distinguish self-inflicted load from a downstream stall.

Map the order-service dependency graph (synchronous downstream calls, shared datastores/queues, shared infrastructure like service mesh or DNS) and enumerate ALL changes across the whole platform in the window 2026-03-17T00:00Z to now: deployments (including order-service v2.15.2 exact rollout time and any other service releases/config changes in the same window), config/flag changes, and any dependency-affecting changes to shared components. For each change list timestamp, service, and what it altered. Include historical incidents resembling 504s on order submit / post-release order failures to see if this is a known pattern.

Correlate the candidate changes found in task b against the exact onset time and affected services found in task a: which change best explains a ~30% order submit failure rate with 504s at that onset? Determine whether order-service v2.15.2 is the likely cause or whether an earlier/other change (e.g., a downstream service deploy, config change to a shared component, or dependency-side degradation) aligns better with the onset and blast radius, and whether rollback would plausibly resolve it.

events.statement: order-service error_rate jumped from a ~0.2% baseline to 19.02% in the 11:00Z bucket and ~30-32% from 11:05Z onward (max 35.57%), sustained through 12:59Z. Onset is in the 11:00:00Z 5-minute bucket; the last pre-onset bucket (10:55Z) was 0.21%, and no earlier bucket exceeded 0.32%.

v2.15.2 rollout completed at 10:48:02Z ("deployment dep-5333 (v2.15.2) rollout complete, all pods ready") and the rollback completed at 11:16:38Z ("rollback of dep-5333 complete, previous version restored"). Onset (11:00Z bucket / first 11:02:45Z error) is ~12 min after the deploy and error_rate stayed ~30% after the rollback, so the symptom neither started at the deploy nor cleared with the rollback.

100% of order-service error logs (349 matched, all level ERROR) carry a single signature: "exchange-gateway call failed: 504 Gateway Timeout (placeOrder)", first_seen 11:02:45Z, last 12:58:54Z. No 4xx, connection-refused or client-timeout signatures appear in the matched set.

exchange-gateway degraded simultaneously and more server-side than order-service: error_rate rose from ~0.2% baseline to 34.8% at 11:00Z and ~43-45% thereafter (max 48.42%), and latency_p99_ms rose from ~130ms baseline to ~5000-5300ms (11:00Z avg 4170.76ms; 11:15Z avg 5235.51ms), sustained through 12:55Z.

order-service is NOT resource-saturated: cpu_pct stayed in a flat 35.72-45.44% band across the whole window (39.21% at 11:00Z, 40.67% at 11:10Z, 38.84% at 12:55Z), and its latency_p99_ms rose from ~150ms baseline to ~5200-5400ms in the same 11:00Z bucket (11:00Z avg 3264.85ms, max 5356.7ms) alongside ~30% errors, which is consistent with the ~5s upstream exchange-gateway timeouts dominating latency rather than local CPU load.

order-service exposes only cpu_pct/db_pool_in_use/error_rate/latency_p99_ms/memory_pct/request_rate/restarts; exchange-gateway exposes those plus upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms. So a deeper downstream dependency of exchange-gateway can be probed via exchange-gateway's upstream_* metrics, which were not yet sampled in this round.

events.description: Could not enumerate the service inventory / dependency graph, so I could not confirm whether payment-service, inventory-service, shipping-service, checkout-service, databases or gateways exist and whether they degraded. Only order-service and exchange-gateway were sampled.
exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms metrics (the natural next hop toward the actual stall) were not queried in this round.

order-service db_pool_in_use, memory_pct, request_rate and restarts were not sampled (only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms); exchange-gateway cpu_pct/memory_pct/request_rate/restarts were not sampled.

No minute-resolution (short-bucket) query was run around 11:00Z; all metric evidence is in 300s buckets, so the onset can only be bounded to the 11:00:00-11:05:00Z bucket, with log-level precision at 11:02:45Z.

events.answer: Order submit failures began in the 11:00Z bucket (first error log 11:02:45Z), i.e. ~12 minutes AFTER the v2.15.2 rollout completed at 10:48:02Z, and persisted through 12:59Z despite the rollback completing at 11:16:38Z - so the failure did not start with the deploy and was not resolved by the rollback. All 349 order-service errors are 504 Gateway Timeout from the call to exchange-gateway on placeOrder; order-service itself is not resource-saturated (CPU flat ~40%), while exchange-gateway shows a simultaneous much larger degradation (error rate ~44%, p99 ~5.1s).

events.statement: order-service dependency graph (caller→callee): api-gateway → order-service → {ledger-db (db), pricing-engine (http), exchange-gateway (http), kafka (queue-produce)}. ledger-db, redis-cache and kafka are flagged shared=true (platform-owned); exchange-api is external with no telemetry. So a neighbour can degrade order-service via the shared ledger-db, kafka, or redis-cache.

pricing-engine (order-service's downstream) itself calls market-data-service (http) and redis-cache (cache), and market-data-service calls redis-cache (cache) and exchange-gateway (http) — a second path by which shared redis-cache or the external exchange can reach order submit.

Exactly one deployment platform-wide in the window 2026-03-17T00:00Z–12:59Z: dep-5333 order-service v2.15.2, deployed_at 2026-03-17T10:48:00Z by a.khan, summary "Add idempotency keys to order submit" (changes: Idempotency-Key header persisted in orders table; retry-safe submit handler), status rolled_back with rolled_back_at 2026-03-17T11:16:00Z — i.e. ~22 min after onset of the report and before the 11:10Z report? No: rollout 10:48Z, rollback 11:16Z, reported 11:10Z.

Exactly one config/flag change platform-wide in the same window: cfg-2290 on pricing-engine, key cache.ttl_seconds changed 5 → 4 at 2026-03-17T09:20:00Z by config-bot ("Shorter quote cache TTL") — ~1.5 h before the order-service rollout.

Targeted checks found NO other changes on dependency-relevant components: ledger-db config changes count=0 and redis-cache config changes count=0 for 2026-03-16T00:00Z–2026-03-17T12:59Z, and pricing-engine deployments count=0 for the same interval.

Historical precedents for 504s on order submit differ in root cause: HIST-103 (2025-10-21, order-service+exchange-gateway, "External exchange API outage on the partner side", category dependency_failure) and HIST-102 (2025-09-02, portfolio-service+ledger-db, "Unplanned ledger-db primary failover; 6 min of refused connections"); also HIST-110 (2026-01-15, order-service+ledger-db, "Cloud volume burst credits exhausted; IOPS throttled" → order latency, statement timeouts) and HIST-116 (2025-12-18, api-gateway, "Envoy upgrade changed HTTP/2 max concurrent streams default", 504 at gateway, category bad_deployment). Past incidents are leads only, and none matches a post-release idempotency-key change.

events.description: No change-history query was run for kafka or for other kafka/ledger-db consumers/fan-in services (only ledger-db and redis-cache config + pricing-engine deployments were checked). get_config_changes was only queried platform-wide (which returned just cfg-2290) plus per-service for ledger-db and redis-cache — kafka itself was not queried individually and could hold changes attributed outside the platform-wide result.

No metric/timeline verification of when order-service errors actually began relative to the 10:48Z rollout and 09:20Z pricing-engine cache TTL change (no metric queries run; this task was scoped to changes/dependencies).

get_config_changes for pricing-engine was not queried individually, so the platform-wide cfg-2290 entry is the only pricing-engine config record available; and api-gateway/exchange-gateway/kafka deployments were not individually enumerated (only the platform-wide 'all services' deployment query was used).

events.answer: order-service sits behind api-gateway and calls pricing-engine and exchange-gateway over HTTP, produces to kafka, and uses the SHARED ledger-db (Postgres) — ledger-db and kafka (and redis-cache, indirectly via pricing-engine/market-data-service) are shared with other services, so neighbours can hurt it. In the incident window (2026-03-17T00:00Z–12:59Z) the platform saw exactly ONE deployment — order-service v2.15.2 (dep-5333, 10:48:00Z, "Add idempotency keys to order submit", rolled back at 11:16:00Z) — and exactly ONE config change — pricing-engine cache.ttl_seconds 5→4 at 09:20:00Z (cfg-2290). No other service releases, no ledger-db/redis-cache config changes, and no pricing-engine deployments were found. This is not identical to any single past incident: the closest precedents for 504s on order submit are HIST-103 (external exchange partner outage) and HIST-102 (ledger-db failover), both different root causes; HIST-110 (ledger-db IOPS throttling) also caused order latency/statement timeouts.

events.statement: The order-service rollout is temporally misaligned with onset: dep-5333 (order-service v2.15.2, "Add idempotency keys to order submit") deployed 10:48:00Z and rolled back 11:16:00Z, while order-service errors began in the 11:00Z bucket (~12 min after rollout) and persisted ~30% after rollback to 12:59Z. A change that causes symptoms neither at its deploy nor cleared by its rollback is a weak fit for root cause.

Blast radius points downstream of order-service, not at it: order-service's 504s and latency are explained by its synchronous HTTP call to exchange-gateway, whose error_rate (~43-45%, max 48.42%) and latency_p99 (~5s) exceed order-service's, while order-service cpu_pct stays flat 35.7-45.4% (no self-inflicted load).

exchange-gateway's only downstream dependency is the external exchange-api (kind external, has_telemetry false, owner vendor): no platform-side dependency of exchange-gateway exists that any in-window deploy/config change touched. This makes a vendor/external degradation the most consistent explanation for the 504 signature 'exchange-gateway call failed: 504 Gateway Timeout (placeOrder)' originating server-side in exchange-gateway.

Platform-wide changes in the window are exhausted: exactly ONE deployment (dep-5333, order-service v2.15.2) and exactly ONE config change (pricing-engine cache.ttl_seconds 5→4 at 09:20Z, cfg-2290) across all services for 2026-03-16T00:00Z-2026-03-17T12:59Z. No change targeted exchange-gateway, exchange-api, ledger-db, kafka or redis-cache.

The pricing-engine config change (cfg-2290, cache TTL 5→4 at 09:20Z) is a poor fit for a ~30% order-submit 504 rate: it is a cache-TTL shortening in a different service path, and it predates onset by ~1h40m, with pricing-engine not appearing in the failing call chain (only exchange-gateway is named in 100% of order-service errors).

Historical precedent HIST-103 (2025-10-21, order-service+exchange-gateway, '504 on order submit' / 'upstream timeouts', category dependency_failure, root cause 'External exchange API outage on the partner side', resolution 'Failed over to secondary exchange route') matches the current symptom set and service pair most closely (match_score 6). This is a lead only, not evidence about the current incident.

events.description: exchange-api is external with has_telemetry=false, so no metrics/logs can confirm whether the vendor partner is degraded (the leading hypothesis); only exchange-gateway's own upstream_error_rate/upstream_latency_ms can proxy it, and those were not sampled in this round.
No telemetry exists for exchange-api and no post-mortem confirms a live partner-side incident for 2026-03-17; HIST-103 is only a similar past incident.

events.answer: No in-window change aligns with the onset or the blast radius. Order-service v2.15.2 (dep-5333) is a weak candidate: it deployed 10:48:00Z, ~12 min BEFORE the 11:00Z onset, and its 11:16:00Z rollback did not clear the ~30% error rate (sustained to 12:59Z); its stated change (idempotency keys on submit) would not produce server-side 504s. The only config change (pricing-engine cache.ttl 5→4 at 09:20Z, cfg-2290) predates onset by ~1h40m and is off the failing path. The best-fitting correlation is a degradation downstream of exchange-gateway: exchange-gateway itself degrades simultaneously but more severely (error_rate ~44%, p99 ~5s) and its sole downstream is the external exchange-api (no telemetry, vendor-owned), matching 100% of order-service's 'exchange-gateway call failed: 504 Gateway Timeout (placeOrder)' errors and the HIST-103 external-partner-outage precedent. Rollback of v2.15.2 would therefore plausibly NOT resolve the incident.

events.title: External exchange-api degradation (vendor side) stalls exchange-gateway, surfacing as 504s on order submit
order-service v2.15.2 idempotency-key release is a bystander (red herring) misaligned with onset and rollback
pricing-engine cache TTL config change (cfg-2290) indirectly destabilizes the quote path
Capacity saturation or resource exhaustion on exchange-gateway / shared component (db pool, memory, connections)

events.summary: H1 (external exchange-api degradation) is the best-fitting hypothesis and clearly outranks H2/H3, which are contradicted by solid evidence (temporal misalignment, post-rollback persistence, downstream 504 signature). However, H1's central hop — that the ~5s stall originates BEYOND exchange-gateway at the external exchange-api — is currently an inference from a dependency-graph fact (exchange-api is exchange-gateway's only dependency) plus a name-based reading of the error text "exchange-gateway call failed: 504". The decisive discriminator between H1 (external vendor) and H4 (capacity saturation inside exchange-gateway) has not been queried: exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate/upstream_latency_ms and its own resource metrics. H4 is not a strawman — F7/F8 establish exchange-gateway is reachable via shared redis-cache/ledger-db/kafka, and a self-inflicted stall would also produce a 504 at exchange-gateway. Two cheap, already-identified queries (F6 explicitly names upstream_* metrics as the natural next hop) can settle this, so this is not inconclusive. Note the framing issue: the "external vendor" label is not verified; if upstream_* metrics are flat while exchange-gateway's own latency is 5s, the origin is INSIDE exchange-gateway (capacity/code) and the fix (and the rollback decision) changes. Also flag: H1 rests partly on HIST-103, a past incident, which is a lead, not current evidence.

events.objective: Decisive H1-vs-H4 test on exchange-gateway: sample exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms over 10:50Z-12:59Z (short buckets if available) and report whether they rise in lockstep with exchange-gateway's own error_rate (~44%) and latency_p99 (~5s) starting in the 11:00Z bucket, or stay flat/baseline while exchange-gateway's own latency is ~5s. Lockstep rise supports H1 (stall beyond exchange-gateway at external exchange-api); flat upstream_* with 5s self-latency points to an internal exchange-gateway fault and changes origin/fix/rollback decision.

Directly test H4 (resource exhaustion / shared-component saturation): sample exchange-gateway cpu_pct, memory_pct, request_rate and any connection/pool or restart metrics over 10:50Z-12:59Z, reporting whether any are elevated/saturated. Also report order-service db_pool_in_use and request_rate over the same window. Flat exchange-gateway resources with 5s stalls strongly contradict H4 and lift H1; saturated resources would invert the ranking. Confirms whether order-service's ~30% has any local pool/load component.

events.statement: exchange-gateway upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms rise in lockstep with its own error_rate/latency_p99_ms, all stepping in the SAME 10:59Z bucket: at 10:56Z upstream_error_rate=0.3% and upstream_latency_ms=117.82ms with self error_rate=0.18% and self latency_p99=129.74ms; by 10:59Z upstream_error_rate avg=15.04 (max 44.52), upstream_latency_ms avg=3140.16 (max 9177.49), self error_rate avg=15.28 (max 45.46), self latency_p99 avg=1809.47 (max 5152.47). They then plateau together: 11:02Z upstream 45.31%/9320.92ms vs self 42.81%/5187.93ms, and at 12:59Z upstream 45.42%/9429.73ms vs self 46.67%/5080.92ms. No bucket shows upstream_* flat while self latency is ~5s.

The upstream (external exchange-api) latency actually EXCEEDS exchange-gateway's own p99 in the same buckets: upstream_latency_ms avg runs ~9,000-9,600ms across 11:02Z-12:59Z (e.g. 11:02Z 9320.92ms, 12:38Z max 10042.78ms, overall max 10042.78) while exchange-gateway latency_p99_ms stays pinned at ~5,000-5,400ms (e.g. 11:02Z 5187.93ms, 11:11Z 5228.14ms, max 5595.57). So the ~5s self-latency is shorter than the upstream stall it wraps — the stall originates at the external call, not inside exchange-gateway.

exchange-gateway shows no internal resource exhaustion during the incident: cpu_pct stays inside a flat 28.56-32.52% band across 10:50Z-12:59Z (29.60% at 10:56Z, 29.15% at 11:02Z, 31.63% at 12:59Z; max 32.52%), and memory_pct stays in a 39.41-48.01% band (43.65% at 10:50Z, 43.83% at 11:02Z, mean 44.08%). Neither rises with the ~9x error-rate jump — arguing against H4 (capacity/resource exhaustion on exchange-gateway).

exchange-gateway's error_rate itself rose in the same 10:59Z bucket as upstream_error_rate (self 0.18% at 10:56Z → 15.28% at 10:59Z → 42.81% at 11:02Z, then ~42-47% through 12:59Z), and its latency_p99 rose 129.74ms → 1809.47ms → 5187.93ms over the same three buckets — i.e. the self-metric onset and the upstream-metric onset are the same 180s bucket, so neither precedes the other at this resolution.
All four metrics returned complete series over 10:50Z-12:59Z with missing_points=0 and partial=false (130 total points each), so the lockstep pattern is not an artifact of missing/sparse data.

events.description: exchange-gateway timeout/abort settings (e.g. why self p99 caps at ~5s while the wrapped upstream call measures ~9.2s) are not exposed as a metric; the exact client-side cut-off config cannot be read from telemetry.

exchange-api (external, has_telemetry=false, owner vendor) exposes no telemetry, so the vendor-side fault itself cannot be directly observed — only the in-platform upstream_* proxy metrics at exchange-gateway.

events.answer: LOCKSTEP — H1 supported, H4 not. exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms rise in the same 10:59Z bucket as its own error_rate and latency_p99_ms, and stay in lockstep through 12:59Z: upstream_error_rate ~0.3% → ~45-46% (max 50.75%), upstream_latency_ms ~117-125ms → ~9,200ms, while self error_rate → ~43-45% and self latency_p99 → ~5,100ms. The stall measures at the external upstream call itself (upstream_latency ~9.2s > self p99 ~5.1s, i.e. the self p99 is the client-abort cut of the longer upstream stall), and exchange-gateway's own cpu_pct (28.6-31.6%) and memory_pct (42-48%) stay flat, so there is no internal exchange-gateway resource exhaustion. This points origin beyond exchange-gateway at the external exchange-api, so rollback of order-service cannot fix it.

events.statement: exchange-gateway cpu_pct is flat and unsaturated across 10:50Z-12:59Z: 29.8% at 10:50Z, 29.87% at 11:02Z, 30.24% at 12:56Z; summary min 26.73, max 32.52, mean 29.85, missing_points 0, total_points 130, partial=false. The ~44% error-rate step in the 10:59Z/11:02Z bucket produced no CPU rise.

exchange-gateway memory_pct is flat and unsaturated across the window: 43.61% at 10:50Z, 45.2% at 11:02Z, 42.8% at 12:56Z; summary min 39.41, max 48.01, mean 44.08, missing_points 0. No memory ramp accompanies the error onset, so no memory-exhaustion signature.

exchange-gateway request_rate shows no load spike: ~270 req/s at 10:50Z, range 245.51-298.46 req/s, mean 274.84 req/s, missing_points 0; there is no queue build-up or traffic surge that could saturate a shared component.

exchange-gateway restarts is 0 for the entire 10:50Z-12:59Z window (every bucket avg 0.0, max 0.0; summary min 0.0, max 0.0, mean 0.0, 130 points). No process restart/OOM-kill occurred, so the ~5s stalls are not crash-restart cycles.

order-service db_pool_in_use is flat and far from saturation across the window: 14.4 conns at 10:50Z, 13.83 at 11:02Z, 13.95 at 12:56Z; min 12.74, max 15.35, mean 14.03, missing_points 0. The connection pool shows no local pool-exhaustion component during the ~30% failure period.

order-service request_rate is flat: 224.17 req/s at 10:50Z, 223.85 at 11:02Z, 227.43 at 12:56Z; min 203.35, max 254.82, mean 232.26 req/s, missing_points 0. The ~30% error rate is not load-driven, i.e. no local request surge component.

events.description: exchange-gateway exposes no connection/pool metric of its own (available_metrics = cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts, upstream_error_rate, upstream_latency_ms), so upstream connection-pool or socket exhaustion inside exchange-gateway cannot be observed directly; only cpu/memory/rate/restarts were available as saturation proxies.
The external exchange-api (dependency type external, has_telemetry=false per F7/F15) has no telemetry, so vendor-side CPU/memory/pool saturation cannot be sampled at the origin.

events.answer: H4 is contradicted. Exchange-gateway's resources and load are all flat/baseline over 10:50Z-12:59Z while its error_rate is ~44% and latency_p99 ~5s: cpu_pct 26.7-32.5% (mean 29.85%), memory_pct 39.4-48.0% (mean 44.08%), request_rate 245.5-298.5 req/s (mean 274.84, no spike), restarts 0 throughout. order-service shows no local pool/load component either: db_pool_in_use 12.74-15.35 conns (mean 14.03, flat) and request_rate 203-255 req/s (mean 232.26, flat) across the ~30% failure window. This lifts H1 (external exchange-api degradation) and confirms order-service's ~30% has no local pool/load component.

events.title: External exchange-api degradation (vendor side) stalls exchange-gateway, surfacing as 504s on order submit
Resource exhaustion / capacity saturation inside exchange-gateway (or a shared component) self-inflicts the 5s stalls
order-service v2.15.2 idempotency-key release is the origin (bad_deployment)
pricing-engine cache TTL config change (cfg-2290) indirectly destabilizes the quote path

events.summary: Round 2 answered the one decisive question from round 1: exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms step in the SAME 10:59Z bucket as its own error_rate/latency_p99 and stay in lockstep to 12:59Z (F19, F22, F23, 130/130 points, missing_points=0), with upstream_latency_ms (~9,000-10,000ms) EXCEEDING exchange-gateway's own p99 (~5,000-5,400ms) (F20). That is exactly the pattern that discriminates H1 from H4: the wrapped upstream call is slower than the self-metric ceiling, so the ~5s is a client-side abort of a longer stall that lives beyond exchange-gateway's own processing, not an internal stall. H4's remaining self-inflicted candidates are contradicted by flat cpu (26.7-32.5%), flat memory (39.4-48.0%), flat request_rate (245-298 req/s, no surge/queue), restarts=0 (F21, F24-F27), and flat order-service cpu/db_pool/request_rate (F5, F28, F29). H2 and H3 remain correctly rejected on temporal misalignment, post-rollback persistence, and error signature (F2, F3, F13, F17). Remaining uncertainty is secondary (which vendor mechanism; the exact configured timeout value) and does not change the origin, the fix direction, or the conclusion that the order-service rollback cannot resolve it. The external-vendor attribution is an inference from upstream_* proxying the sole external dependency (F15) rather than direct vendor telemetry; that caps confidence rather than blocking acceptance. Wrap as: external/partner-side degradation behind exchange-gateway (HIST-103 pattern), order-service rollback irrelevant, escalate to vendor / fail over to secondary exchange route. A peer sampler for order-service cpu/memory/request_rate/restarts would satisfy the gap completely, but the current sample (cpu, error_rate, latency_p99, db_pool_in_use, request_rate) is enough because the latch that clears H1-vs-H4 is server-side consistency between upstream_* and self metrics.

events.why: top hypothesis is above threshold and clearly ahead

tasks.objective: Establish the precise symptom timeline and blast radius for the order-service failure: when exactly did order submit error rate and 504s begin (minute-level onset, and did it start before or after the v2.15.2 rollout?), which order-service endpoints/error signatures dominate (504 vs 4xx vs timeouts vs connection refused), and which other services show simultaneous error/latency/resource degradation (upstream callers, downstream payment/inventory/shipping/checkout, databases, gateways). Also report resource trends (CPU, memory, connection pools, saturation) for order-service and any service it calls, to distinguish self-inflicted load from a downstream stall.
tasks.answer: Order submit failures began in the 11:00Z bucket (first error log 11:02:45Z), i.e. ~12 minutes AFTER the v2.15.2 rollout completed at 10:48:02Z, and persisted through 12:59Z despite the rollback completing at 11:16:38Z - so the failure did not start with the deploy and was not resolved by the rollback. All 349 order-service errors are 504 Gateway Timeout from the call to exchange-gateway on placeOrder; order-service itself is not resource-saturated (CPU flat ~40%), while exchange-gateway shows a simultaneous much larger degradation (error rate ~44%, p99 ~5.1s).

tasks.objective: Map the order-service dependency graph (synchronous downstream calls, shared datastores/queues, shared infrastructure like service mesh or DNS) and enumerate ALL changes across the whole platform in the window 2026-03-17T00:00Z to now: deployments (including order-service v2.15.2 exact rollout time and any other service releases/config changes in the same window), config/flag changes, and any dependency-affecting changes to shared components. For each change list timestamp, service, and what it altered. Include historical incidents resembling 504s on order submit / post-release order failures to see if this is a known pattern.
tasks.answer: order-service sits behind api-gateway and calls pricing-engine and exchange-gateway over HTTP, produces to kafka, and uses the SHARED ledger-db (Postgres) — ledger-db and kafka (and redis-cache, indirectly via pricing-engine/market-data-service) are shared with other services, so neighbours can hurt it. In the incident window (2026-03-17T00:00Z–12:59Z) the platform saw exactly ONE deployment — order-service v2.15.2 (dep-5333, 10:48:00Z, "Add idempotency keys to order submit", rolled back at 11:16:00Z) — and exactly ONE config change — pricing-engine cache.ttl_seconds 5→4 at 09:20:00Z (cfg-2290). No other service releases, no ledger-db/redis-cache config changes, and no pricing-engine deployments were found. This is not identical to any single past incident: the closest precedents for 504s on order submit are HIST-103 (external exchange partner outage) and HIST-102 (ledger-db failover), both different root causes; HIST-110 (ledger-db IOPS throttling) also caused order latency/statement timeouts.

tasks.objective: Correlate the candidate changes found in task b against the exact onset time and affected services found in task a: which change best explains a ~30% order submit failure rate with 504s at that onset? Determine whether order-service v2.15.2 is the likely cause or whether an earlier/other change (e.g., a downstream service deploy, config change to a shared component, or dependency-side degradation) aligns better with the onset and blast radius, and whether rollback would plausibly resolve it.
tasks.answer: No in-window change aligns with the onset or the blast radius. Order-service v2.15.2 (dep-5333) is a weak candidate: it deployed 10:48:00Z, ~12 min BEFORE the 11:00Z onset, and its 11:16:00Z rollback did not clear the ~30% error rate (sustained to 12:59Z); its stated change (idempotency keys on submit) would not produce server-side 504s. The only config change (pricing-engine cache.ttl 5→4 at 09:20Z, cfg-2290) predates onset by ~1h40m and is off the failing path. The best-fitting correlation is a degradation downstream of exchange-gateway: exchange-gateway itself degrades simultaneously but more severely (error_rate ~44%, p99 ~5s) and its sole downstream is the external exchange-api (no telemetry, vendor-owned), matching 100% of order-service's 'exchange-gateway call failed: 504 Gateway Timeout (placeOrder)' errors and the HIST-103 external-partner-outage precedent. Rollback of v2.15.2 would therefore plausibly NOT resolve the incident.

tasks.objective: Decisive H1-vs-H4 test on exchange-gateway: sample exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms over 10:50Z-12:59Z (short buckets if available) and report whether they rise in lockstep with exchange-gateway's own error_rate (~44%) and latency_p99 (~5s) starting in the 11:00Z bucket, or stay flat/baseline while exchange-gateway's own latency is ~5s. Lockstep rise supports H1 (stall beyond exchange-gateway at external exchange-api); flat upstream_* with 5s self-latency points to an internal exchange-gateway fault and changes origin/fix/rollback decision.
tasks.answer: LOCKSTEP — H1 supported, H4 not. exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms rise in the same 10:59Z bucket as its own error_rate and latency_p99_ms, and stay in lockstep through 12:59Z: upstream_error_rate ~0.3% → ~45-46% (max 50.75%), upstream_latency_ms ~117-125ms → ~9,200ms, while self error_rate → ~43-45% and self latency_p99 → ~5,100ms. The stall measures at the external upstream call itself (upstream_latency ~9.2s > self p99 ~5.1s, i.e. the self p99 is the client-abort cut of the longer upstream stall), and exchange-gateway's own cpu_pct (28.6-31.6%) and memory_pct (42-48%) stay flat, so there is no internal exchange-gateway resource exhaustion. This points origin beyond exchange-gateway at the external exchange-api, so rollback of order-service cannot fix it.

tasks.objective: Directly test H4 (resource exhaustion / shared-component saturation): sample exchange-gateway cpu_pct, memory_pct, request_rate and any connection/pool or restart metrics over 10:50Z-12:59Z, reporting whether any are elevated/saturated. Also report order-service db_pool_in_use and request_rate over the same window. Flat exchange-gateway resources with 5s stalls strongly contradict H4 and lift H1; saturated resources would invert the ranking. Confirms whether order-service's ~30% has any local pool/load component.
tasks.answer: H4 is contradicted. Exchange-gateway's resources and load are all flat/baseline over 10:50Z-12:59Z while its error_rate is ~44% and latency_p99 ~5s: cpu_pct 26.7-32.5% (mean 29.85%), memory_pct 39.4-48.0% (mean 44.08%), request_rate 245.5-298.5 req/s (mean 274.84, no spike), restarts 0 throughout. order-service shows no local pool/load component either: db_pool_in_use 12.74-15.35 conns (mean 14.03, flat) and request_rate 203-255 req/s (mean 232.26, flat) across the ~30% failure window. This lifts H1 (external exchange-api degradation) and confirms order-service's ~30% has no local pool/load component.

critiques.summary: H1 (external exchange-api degradation) is the best-fitting hypothesis and clearly outranks H2/H3, which are contradicted by solid evidence (temporal misalignment, post-rollback persistence, downstream 504 signature). However, H1's central hop — that the ~5s stall originates BEYOND exchange-gateway at the external exchange-api — is currently an inference from a dependency-graph fact (exchange-api is exchange-gateway's only dependency) plus a name-based reading of the error text "exchange-gateway call failed: 504". The decisive discriminator between H1 (external vendor) and H4 (capacity saturation inside exchange-gateway) has not been queried: exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate/upstream_latency_ms and its own resource metrics. H4 is not a strawman — F7/F8 establish exchange-gateway is reachable via shared redis-cache/ledger-db/kafka, and a self-inflicted stall would also produce a 504 at exchange-gateway. Two cheap, already-identified queries (F6 explicitly names upstream_* metrics as the natural next hop) can settle this, so this is not inconclusive. Note the framing issue: the "external vendor" label is not verified; if upstream_* metrics are flat while exchange-gateway's own latency is 5s, the origin is INSIDE exchange-gateway (capacity/code) and the fix (and the rollback decision) changes. Also flag: H1 rests partly on HIST-103, a past incident, which is a lead, not current evidence.

challenges.issue: The hop 'external exchange-api stalls ~5s' is not verified by any finding. F15 is an inference from the dependency graph (exchange-gateway's only downstream is external exchange-api), and the 504 text 'exchange-gateway call failed' is emitted by exchange-gateway's own caller-facing surface — it does not distinguish 'downstream timed out' from 'exchange-gateway itself timed out internally'. The decisive proxy (exchange-gateway upstream_error_rate / upstream_latency_ms, F6) was never sampled.

F18/HIST-103 (a 2025 external-partner outage with match_score 6) is used as corroboration. It is a past incident and, by the dependency agent's own statement, 'a lead only, not evidence about the current incident'. It must not raise confidence in H1.

H4 is dismissed largely by absence ('only CPU verified flat'). exchange-gateway's cpu/memory/request_rate/pool metrics were never sampled, and F7/F8 put shared redis-cache/ledger-db/kafka on paths that can reach exchange-gateway. A self-inflicted 5s stall inside exchange-gateway reproduces every piece of current evidence equally well. One hop of its chain is admittedly unevidenced.

Onset-direction/ordering: both exchange-gateway and order-service are pinned to the same 300s bucket (11:00Z), so 'exchange-gateway degraded first, order-service inherited' is asserted, not shown. Granularity permits one lagging the other by up to ~5 min either way.

Scope: rollback of v2.15.2 is proceeding on the assumption the cause is external. If H1's external-origin hop fails verification, an internal exchange-gateway fault would be mislabeled vendor-side and escalate incorrectly. The 'external vendor, no telemetry' conclusion should not be stated as established.

Do they rise in lockstep with exchange-gateway's own error_rate (~44%) and latency_p99 (~5s) starting in the 11:00Z bucket, or do they stay flat/baseline while exchange-gateway's own latency is 5s?
evidence_requests.rationale: This is the single decisive test between H1 (stall beyond exchange-gateway at external exchange-api) and H4 (stall inside exchange-gateway). Lockstep rise supports H1; flat upstream_* with 5s self latency points to an internal exchange-gateway fault/capacity issue and changes the origin, the fix and the rollback decision. F6 confirms these metrics exist and were not yet sampled in this round.

critiques.summary: Round 2 answered the one decisive question from round 1: exchange-gateway's upstream_error_rate and upstream_latency_ms step in the SAME 10:59Z bucket as its own error_rate/latency_p99 and stay in lockstep to 12:59Z (F19, F22, F23, 130/130 points, missing_points=0), with upstream_latency_ms (~9,000-10,000ms) EXCEEDING exchange-gateway's own p99 (~5,000-5,400ms) (F20). That is exactly the pattern that discriminates H1 from H4: the wrapped upstream call is slower than the self-metric ceiling, so the ~5s is a client-side abort of a longer stall that lives beyond exchange-gateway's own processing, not an internal stall. H4's remaining self-inflicted candidates are contradicted by flat cpu (26.7-32.5%), flat memory (39.4-48.0%), flat request_rate (245-298 req/s, no surge/queue), restarts=0 (F21, F24-F27), and flat order-service cpu/db_pool/request_rate (F5, F28, F29). H2 and H3 remain correctly rejected on temporal misalignment, post-rollback persistence, and error signature (F2, F3, F13, F17). Remaining uncertainty is secondary (which vendor mechanism; the exact configured timeout value) and does not change the origin, the fix direction, or the conclusion that the order-service rollback cannot resolve it. The external-vendor attribution is an inference from upstream_* proxying the sole external dependency (F15) rather than direct vendor telemetry; that caps confidence rather than blocking acceptance. Wrap as: external/partner-side degradation behind exchange-gateway (HIST-103 pattern), order-service rollback irrelevant, escalate to vendor / fail over to secondary exchange route. A peer sampler for order-service cpu/memory/request_rate/restarts would satisfy the gap completely, but the current sample (cpu, error_rate, latency_p99, db_pool_in_use, request_rate) is enough because the latch that clears H1-vs-H4 is server-side consistency between upstream_* and self metrics.

challenges.issue: Origin label 'external exchange-api' is inferred, not directly observed: exchange-api has has_telemetry=false, so no vendor-side metric, log, or partner status page confirms a vendor incident. The chain rests on exchange-gateway's upstream_* metrics as a proxy (F19/F20) plus the dependency fact that exchange-api is exchange-gateway's only downstream (F15). The proxy is strong (upstream_latency ~9-10s > self p99 ~5s, lockstep onset, complete series), so this is a naming/granularity caveat on an established origin, not an unresolved origin — fix direction (vendor escalation / secondary route failover, not order-service) is unchanged either way.

Timeout mechanism is asserted, not measured: the claim that exchange-gateway's ~5s p99 is a client-abort cut of the ~9-10s upstream stall is arithmetically consistent but the configured timeout value is not exposed as a metric (open gap). This closes the story only aesthetically; the relative magnitudes already localize the delay at the external call.

Onset direction cannot be pinned below 300s buckets: self and upstream metrics both step in the same 10:59Z bucket (F19/F22), so 'upstream first vs self first' is unresolved at this resolution. This does not affect origin, since F20 (upstream latency exceeding self p99 in the same buckets) already forces the delayed hop to be upstream of exchange-gateway's own processing regardless of which sample bucket lit first.

Residual un-excluded internal path: exchange-gateway exposes no connection/socket pool metric, so upstream socket-pool exhaustion inside exchange-gateway cannot be directly observed (only cpu/mem/rate/restarts as proxies). A pool stall is a plausible mechanism for a ~5s cut but fits the flat request_rate/restarts and consistent lockstep less cleanly than an external stall; it also lies upstream of exchange-gateway's own request handling, so it would not change the fix direction toward order-service.

Blast-radius enumeration incomplete: only order-service and exchange-gateway were sampled; other callers of exchange-gateway (e.g., market-data-service via F8, checkout/payment callers of order-service) were not sampled, so a shared external origin is not corroborated by other victims.
